ci_method: Anderson-Rubin weak-instrument-robust 95% confidence set, obtained by inverting the heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) AR test over a grid of candidate betas from -500 to 500 in steps of 0.001 and comparing to the chi2(1) 95% critical value (3.8415). The resulting set is contiguous and bounded: [-0.051, 1.804]. Cross-checked three ways: (a) independently re-estimated in R (identical set, [-0.050, 1.800] on a 0.005 grid); (b) closed-form algebraic inversion of the homoskedastic AR quadratic, giving [-0.008, 1.643]; (c) AR using the F(1, n-4) rather than chi2(1) critical value, giving [-0.051, 1.829]. AR is used instead of the conventional 2SLS Wald interval because the instrument is weak (first-stage robust F = 4.22), which makes the Wald interval's 95% coverage invalid; AR retains correct coverage for any instrument strength and is the optimal weak-IV-robust test in a just-identified model. For reference, the naive 2SLS Wald interval would be [0.018, 0.408] and the tF-adjusted (Lee, McCrary, Moreira & Porter 2022) interval is [-0.897, 1.323]; both the AR and tF intervals contain zero.

assumptions_checked: INSTRUMENT RELEVANCE - FAILS. First-stage robust F on dist_college_miles is 4.22 (homoskedastic 4.39), partial R2 = 0.0029. This is below the conventional rule-of-thumb of 10, below the Stock-Yogo critical value of 16.38 (one instrument, 10% maximal size distortion), and far below the F = 104.7 that Lee, McCrary, Moreira & Porter (2022) show is required for a conventional 95% 2SLS t-interval to actually have 95% coverage. The raw correlation between distance and schooling is only -0.058. This is the binding problem with the design.

WEAK-INSTRUMENT-ROBUST INFERENCE - done because relevance fails. Inverted the robust Anderson-Rubin test to get a 95% set of [-0.051, 1.804], which contains zero. Also computed the tF-adjusted interval [-0.897, 1.323], which contains zero. The AR set is bounded but only knife-edge so: a bounded AR interval requires first-stage partial R2 > 1/(dof/crit + 1) = 0.00257, and the actual partial R2 is 0.00293, exceeding the threshold by only a factor of 1.14. Slightly less signal and the 95% set would have been infinite.

TEST THAT THE EFFECT IS ZERO - cannot reject. In a just-identified model the AR test of beta=0 is exactly the reduced-form test of the instrument, which gives p = 0.072. So at the 5% level the data do not reject the hypothesis of no causal effect of schooling on wages.

INSTRUMENT EXOGENEITY / EXCLUSION - partially probed, fundamentally untestable here. Checked balance of the instrument on the two pre-determined covariates: dist_college_miles does not predict parent_educ (coef=-0.0041, p=0.396) or female (coef=0.0005, p=0.616), which is mildly reassuring. Ran a Sargan over-identification test after adding dist^2 as a second instrument: chi2(1)=1.85, p=0.174, no rejection - but this is weak evidence because both instruments are weak and Sargan cannot test exclusion in the just-identified baseline. The substantive threats remain unaddressed by the data: distance to college is plausibly correlated with rural/urban residence, local labour-market quality and local wage levels, which affect wages directly. The dataset has no geography, cohort or local-labour-market controls, so the exclusion restriction cannot be defended with these variables alone.

ENDOGENEITY OF SCHOOLING - cannot reject exogeneity. Durbin chi2(1)=0.861 (p=0.353), Wu-Hausman F=0.859 (p=0.354), Wooldridge regression test chi2(1)=0.820 (p=0.365), and the control-function augmented regression in R gives a coefficient on the first-stage residual of -0.086 (p=0.366). So there is no statistical evidence here that OLS is biased - though this test has very low power precisely because the instrument is weak, so it is not affirmative support for using OLS either.

OLS vs 2SLS COMPARISON. 2SLS (0.213) is about 1.7x OLS (0.128), and the AR test does not reject the OLS value either (AR stat at beta=0.128 is 0.814, p=0.367). The gap is not statistically distinguishable from zero and is well within what weak-instrument noise produces, so it should not be read as evidence of ability bias in a particular direction.

HETEROSKEDASTICITY. Breusch-Pagan on the OLS residuals gives LM=0.886, p=0.829, so no evidence of heteroskedasticity; HC1-robust standard errors were used throughout anyway and are nearly identical to homoskedastic ones (2SLS se 0.0994 robust vs 0.1008 unadjusted).

SPECIFICATION STABILITY - poor. The 2SLS point estimate moves over roughly 0.15 to 0.45 across control sets and subsamples, and the first stage is fragile: it disappears for women alone (F=0.40) and collapses when the 23 observations beyond 60 miles are trimmed (F drops from 4.22 to 1.65, point estimate moves to 0.345). The identifying variation rests on a thin tail of long-distance observations.

DATA QUALITY. 1500 rows, no missing values in any variable, no duplicate person_id. years_school ranges 8-19 with a sensible unimodal distribution, parent_educ 6-18, distance 0.1-103.4 miles, 46% female. No coding anomalies found.

FUNCTIONAL FORM / MONOTONE LINEAR FIRST STAGE. Tried log(dist+1) and a 1[dist<10] indicator as alternative instruments; both are weaker (F=1.74 and F=0.87), so the weak first stage is not an artefact of imposing linearity in miles.

ESTIMATOR SENSITIVITY. LIML is identical to 2SLS (as it must be when just-identified) and Fuller(1), which has better weak-instrument finite-sample properties, gives 0.197 - close to 2SLS, so the headline number is not an artefact of the 2SLS bias correction choice.
headline_claim: Instrumenting schooling with distance to college in these data does not identify the return to schooling: the instrument is weak (first-stage F = 4.2, far below any accepted threshold), and the weak-instrument-robust 95% confidence interval for the effect of an extra year of schooling runs from -0.05 to 1.80 and includes zero, so while the 2SLS point estimate is 0.213 log points the data cannot distinguish a zero return from an implausibly enormous one.
